     2|
     3|*A Memoir by Robert Mills*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|### Transition: From Bobs Childhood to the Spark of Sputnik
     8|
     9|The summer the dog died, something shifted in Bob's brain that he would not understand for decades. The hippocampus—the seahorse-shaped structure deep in the temporal lobe responsible for encoding memories—had filed away the image of the black mongrel with the white-tipped tail as both comfort and loss. Neural pathways that had linked the dog's presence to safety and playfulness now carried a new signal: that love could be taken without warning. At seven, Bob's amygdala learned its first profound lesson. The world was not entirely safe, and the creatures who filled it could vanish without permission.
    10|
    11|Grief, at that age, is experienced not as a philosophical problem but as a physical one. Cortisol levels rise, sustained by the constant low-grade awareness that something important is missing. The nervous system enters a state of hypervigilance, scanning the environment for the lost object, the absent friend. Bob would find himself listening for the scrape of paws against the back door, looking up from his toys at sounds that did not contain what his brain insisted was coming. The body grieves in its own way, through its own channels, long before the mind has the vocabulary to articulate what loss means. Every morning when Bob opened his eyes, the moment before memory kicked in was a moment of peace—a fraction of a second where the world still contained his dog. Then memory arrived, and with it came the weight of absence, the weight of a silence where there should have been a bark.
    12|
    13|That autumn, the beeping began. It came from a radio console in his grandparents' living room, a mahogany cabinet of vacuum tubes and glowing filaments that dominated the room like a mechanical altar. The voice spoke of Russians, of a silver sphere circling the Earth. Beep. Beep. Beep. For Bob, sitting cross-legged on the worn linoleum, it triggered something his developing brain could not yet name. Psychologists would later call these flashbulb memories—vivid recollections encoded during times of intense emotion or historical significance, burned into the hippocampus with the permanence of a brand. For Bob and his generation, Sputnik became exactly that.
    14|
    15|The contrast between the dog's death and Sputnik's arrival was physiological as well as emotional. Where grief had elevated cortisol and activated the sympathetic nervous system, wonder released dopamine in the ventral striatum, triggered by novelty and possibility, creating pathways that pointed not backward toward loss but forward toward discovery. The same brain that had learned death could also learn wonder. Both experiences were woven into the fabric of his developing identity—one teaching vulnerability, the other aspiration.
    16|
    17|America in 1957 was experiencing its own version of what Bob's amygdala had just learned. The Space Race was a collective nervous system response to the unknown. What it meant for a child of the Midwest to hear that beeping from a distant world was to absorb, in embryonic form, the understanding that possibility was wider than the boundaries of his street.
    18|
    19|### Transition: From Sputnik to the Family Legacy in the Garage
    20|
    21|Between the cosmic beeping of Sputnik and the practical building of Bob's childhood lay a gap he would spend decades bridging: the space between dreaming about the impossible and learning to make the possible. Sputnik had given his generation permission to imagine reaching the stars. But the actual work began in garages where fathers and sons bent over workbenches and learned that wonder required competence.
    22|
    23|When a child observes a parent building something, mirror neurons in the premotor cortex fire in sympathetic patterns, rehearsing the same motor sequences even when the child's hands remain still. Bob was not merely watching his father build; his brain was building a template for building itself. Every Saturday in the garage was a masterclass in embodied cognition—the process by which the brain learns through direct interaction with physical reality rather than abstract instruction.
    24|
    25|The garage represented the certainty of achievable mastery. Sputnik was distant, controlled by governments. The garage was immediate, personal—a father and son with a scroll saw and an afternoon. Where the cosmic beeping had activated the amygdala's capacity for wonder, the garage activated the prefrontal cortex's capacity for planning and execution. The same nervous system that had learned to look up at the sky and dream was now learning to look down at a piece of wood and understand what it could become.
    26|
    27|Bob's father had returned from war with skills that were practical, physical, rooted in circuits and engines that could be touched and repaired. In an era when America was pivoting toward the abstract complexity of rocket science, the garage preserved something older: the direct relationship between human hands and physical materials. It was the garage that taught Bob the foundational truth every engineer needs: that things can be built, that broken things can be repaired, that understanding comes from doing.

Part One: The Ignition

Chapter One: The Shock

82| 83|
Summer 1958, Northern Michigan
84| 85|

The summer of 1958 arrived in Michigan like all the others before it—warm, languid, scented with pine and lake water. For six-year-old Bob, this summer marked something else entirely: the precise moment when memory begins, crystalline and sharp, or so he would come to believe.

86| 87|

The family had traveled north to a modest cabin nestled among the woods, a ritual escape from the sweltering heat of the lower peninsula. Bob's father had secured some time away from work, no small feat in those years, and the family packed themselves into the car with the practiced efficiency of people who had learned to make do with little. The cabin was simple—wooden walls, a small kitchen, bedrooms that smelled of cedar and mothballs—but to a child of six, it contained universes of possibility.

88| 89|

On this particular afternoon, the adults had retreated to the front room, their voices a low murmur of adult conversation that signaled safety and boredom in equal measure. Bob was alone in the kitchen, a space transformed by his solitude into something approaching a laboratory—full of drawers to open, cabinets to explore, and mysteries yet undiscovered.

90| 91|

His father's car keys lay on the counter, abandoned in the transition from arrival to settling in. They were ordinary keys, the kind any man might carry in 1958, but they bore an adornment that captured Bob's complete attention: a Native American puzzle fob. The fob was intricate, a small wooden object carved with geometric precision, its pieces interlocking in ways that suggested both order and mystery to a curious young mind.

92| 93|

Bob picked up the keys. The metal felt cool against his palm. He turned the fob over and over, studying the way the pieces fit together, wondering at the cleverness of whoever had designed such a thing. His fingers traced the carved surfaces, finding the slight ridges where tool had met wood.

94| 95|

But childhood curiosity is a restless thing, never satisfied with a single mystery when another might lie nearby. As Bob twisted the puzzle fob, his eyes wandered upward, scanning the kitchen walls until they found what they sought: an electrical outlet.

96| 97|

Bob knew about electrical outlets. He had heard the warnings—parents in 1958 were no less vigilant about such dangers than they are today, perhaps more so in an era before ground fault interrupters and child-safety covers. The words had been spoken: "Don't put things in the outlet." But words are abstract things to a six-year-old, weightless concepts that lack the gravity of experience. The allure of the outlet was not defiance, exactly. It was something more primal—the same impulse that sends children to poke sticks into streams, to peer down wells, to press their faces against aquarium glass. The outlet was a mystery. The keys were in his hand. And in the mind of a curious child, these two facts began to form a question that demanded an answer. What would happen?

98| 99|

The memory, if memory it is, plays out with the slowness of a dream. Bob gripping the key—not the fob end, but the metal shaft. His small hand extending toward the outlet. The twin slots waiting, dark and silent and full of promise. What happened next would become the foundational moment of Bob's life, the first chapter in a story that would unfold across seven decades. The key made contact.

100| 101|

Electricity is invisible. We see its effects—light, heat, motion—but the current itself remains hidden, a ghost in the walls. In that moment, six-year-old Bob met this invisible force directly, unfiltered, raw. The shock surged through his body with the indifference of physics acting upon matter. His muscles contracted involuntarily, a puppet's dance with invisible strings. The force threw him backward—"catapulted," he would later think of it, though at six he possessed no such vocabulary. He flew several feet across the kitchen, landing in a heap against the far wall.

102| 103|

Darkness. Not the gentle dark of bedtime, but a violent absence of sight. His heart hammered against his ribs like something trying to escape. His hand—oh, his hand—tingled with a strange, persistent vibration that seemed to echo the current that had passed through it. Time dilated. Those agonizing moments of disorientation stretched into what felt like hours, though they were likely only seconds. Bob sat in a daze, grappling with the reality of what had just occurred. His body had touched something invisible and been punished for it. The world had revealed one of its hidden rules.

104| 105|

Then came the footsteps—hurried, panicked. His parents burst into the kitchen, their faces transformed by concern and confusion. They found their son crumpled against the wall, the keys lying on the floor between him and the outlet, the connection obvious even without explanation. The scolding came, as scoldings do. Words of admonishment, expressions of fear dressed in anger. Bob was told what he already knew, what his body had learned in the most direct way possible: electricity was dangerous. The warnings, so abstract before, had found their weight. And yet…

106| 107|

Here is where the memory, if memory it is, takes an unexpected turn. Despite the terror of the moment, despite the scolding that followed, six-year-old Bob felt something else entirely. The experience was terrifying, yes, but it was also—exhilarating. The shock had been a revelation. In touching that outlet, Bob had reached beyond the ordinary boundaries of childhood into a realm of invisible forces and physical laws. He had asked a question of the universe—what will happen?—and the universe had answered with unmistakable clarity. The pain was real. The fear was real. But so too was the learning, immediate and visceral, in a way that no textbook or parental warning could ever achieve. This was science. This was discovery. This was the moment when a child realizes that the world operates according to principles that can be tested, that cause leads to effect with mathematical precision, that even the most dire warnings cannot compare to the power of direct experience.

108| 109|
The Memory of Memory
110| 111|

But here we must pause. Because Bob, looking back across sixty years from the vantage of the present, can never be entirely certain that this memory belongs to him. The mind is a trickster. Cognitive psychologists have established this with certainty: every time we recall a memory, we reconstruct it. The act of remembering alters the memory itself, like a document being retyped with slight variations each time. Details shift. Emotions intensify or fade. The boundary between what actually happened and what we believe happened becomes porous, permeable, eventually indistinguishable. Bob's mother told the story of the electrical outlet many times as he grew up. She would recount it at family gatherings, using it as a cautionary tale for younger cousins, shaking her head at her son's reckless curiosity. With each retelling, the story gained texture—Bob's fascination with the puzzle fob, the exact sound of his body hitting the wall, the expression on his father's face when he entered the room. Did Bob remember these things? Or did he remember his mother remembering them? The memory he carries feels real—the tingling hand, the taste of fear, the strange exhilaration that followed. But feeling real and being real are different things. A false memory can feel as vivid, as certain, as one formed from actual experience.

112| 113|
The Science of Uncertainty
114| 115|

This uncertainty—the impossibility of knowing whether the memory is genuine or constructed—would haunt Bob throughout his life. It became a lens through which he examined all his recollections, a nagging doubt that colored every "I remember when." Was his memory of that first day of school authentic? His memory of his grandfather's voice? His memory of anything? The memories that shaped his personality, his fears, his desires—how many of them were borrowed from photographs, from stories, from the collective mythology of family? From his own foggy memories? The electrical outlet incident, real or reconstructed, became the cornerstone of Bob's "memory palace"—the mental architecture where he stored his most significant experiences. But unlike other memories that gradually clarified with age, this one remained stubbornly ambiguous. It existed in a quantum state, simultaneously real and imagined, its truth dependent entirely on the observer.

116| 117|
The Spark That Ignited
118| 119|

What is not ambiguous is the effect this event had on the course of Bob's life. Whether he actually felt that jolt of electricity or merely believed he had, the result was the same: an awakening. The experience ignited something in Bob—a fascination with electricity that would evolve into a passion for science and technology. In the months and years that followed, he devoured books on electrical circuits with the hunger of someone who had tasted the power hidden in walls and wished to understand it. He conducted home experiments, some dangerous, all illuminating. He built gadgets from scrap parts, learning through trial and error the principles that governed the invisible force that had once thrown him across a kitchen. His parents, perhaps recognizing that his curiosity could not be extinguished—only channeled—nurtured his scientific endeavors. They bought him books. They tolerated the mess of his experiments. They learned to check the fuse box after he had been "working" in the basement. This passion led to academic excellence in science, which led to university, which led to degrees in electrical and systems engineering. The little boy who had touched the outlet grew into a man who would help design systems for NASA, who would contemplate missions to Mars, who would spend his professional life facing toward the stars.

120| 121|
The Metaphor
122| 123|

But the gift of the electrical outlet incident was not merely vocational. It was philosophical. The memory—if memory it is—taught Bob something fundamental about the nature of knowledge. It taught him that understanding requires risk, that the pursuit of truth sometimes demands that we touch the very things we're warned against, that learning is not always safe or comfortable. It taught him about the malleability of memory itself. His uncertainty about the authenticity of the experience led him to study the neuroscience of recollection, to understand concepts like "reconsolidation" and the construction of false memories. He learned that human memory is not a video recording but an active, creative process—a story we tell ourselves about ourselves, subject to revision with each telling. Most importantly, it taught him that the most formative moments of our lives might be partly—or entirely—fictional, and yet remain no less powerful for it. Whether Bob actually touched that outlet and felt that shock matters less than the fact that he believes he did, that this belief shaped his curiosity, his career, his very identity.

124| 125|
The Loop
126| 127|

Now, as Bob stands in his seventh decade looking backward through the telescope of time, the electrical outlet incident remains his earliest memory—or his earliest believed memory. It sits at the foundation of everything that followed, the first domino in a cascade that created the man he would become. He has studied the brain since then. He knows about synaptic plasticity and long-term potentiation. He understands that memories form when neurons fire in patterns, strengthening their connections through repetition and emotional significance. He knows that strong emotions—like the fear and wonder of that moment in the kitchen—create particularly vivid memories, etched deep into the hippocampus and the amygdala. But knowing the mechanism does not resolve the mystery. Bob still cannot say with certainty whether he remembers the shock itself or only remembers his mother telling him about it. The memory remains stubbornly dual, existing in two states at once, a quantum superposition of real and imagined. Perhaps that is fitting. Perhaps the ambiguity itself is the lesson—the recognition that our pasts are not fixed things but ongoing creations, stories we revise as we age, meanings we make from events that may or may not have occurred exactly as we recall them.

128| 129|
The Beginning
130| 131|

So this is where we begin: with a six-year-old boy in a Michigan cabin, holding his father's keys. With a moment of curiosity that crossed a boundary. With a shock that may or may not have happened exactly as remembered, but that changed everything regardless. The outlet still waits in the wall of memory, dark and full of promise. The key still hangs in the air, metal gleaming, poised between innocence and experience. The child still sits on that far kitchen floor, heart pounding, hand tingling, eyes wide with the terror and wonder of discovery. Whether it happened or not, it is true. It is the creation myth of a life, the spark that lit a flame that still burns sixty years later. It is the first chapter of a story about memory and identity, about how the past creates the present creates the future in an endless loop of becoming. The shock was literal, perhaps. Or it was metaphorical. Or it was both. But its effect was undeniable. It launched a boy across a kitchen and into a life of inquiry, a life spent reaching toward mysteries just beyond the fingertips, trusting that the answers—even when they shock us—are worth the seeking. In the end, it doesn't matter whether Bob remembers that day or only remembers remembering it. The memory has done its work. It has shaped a human being who would spend his life questioning, exploring, wondering—who would never accept that the walls contain nothing more than wires, who would always suspect that just behind the ordinary surface of things lies something extraordinary, waiting to be touched. The outlet waits. The key turns. The story begins.

132| 133|

That electrical spark—the literal shock and the metaphorical awakening it ignited—would have to wait for its perfect complement when something far more distant than a kitchen outlet began to beep its way across the night sky. The child who had touched invisible forces in a Michigan cabin was eventually to discover that the universe itself was reaches that extended far beyond anything he could yet imagine.

# Book Deliverable — KDP Publishing Package

Complete workflow for packaging a finished book manuscript for Amazon KDP submission.

## Prerequisites
- Finished manuscript (`.md`)
- Cover image (PNG, any ratio — gets resized)
- Output directory containing HTML/EPUB/PDF builds

## Step-by-Step

### 1. Check Page Count
```bash
pdfinfo output/{FILE_PREFIX}.pdf | grep Pages
```

### 2. Create Kindle Cover JPEG (1600×2560px)
```python
from PIL import Image
img = Image.open('{BOOK_KEY}_Cover.png')
resized = img.resize((1600, 2560), Image.LANCZOS)
resized.convert('RGB').save('generated_images/{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_Kindle_Cover.jpg', 'JPEG', quality=95)
```

### 3. Build KDP Package

Run the packaged build script:

```bash
python3 build_kdp_package.py
```

This script does everything:
- **Kindle/**: Copies EPUB + 1600×2560 JPEG cover
- **Print/**: Generates print-ready PDF (6×9in + 0.125in bleeds), wrap cover (front+spine+back) as JPEG + PDF
- **Marketing_and_Compliance/**: Book description, author bio, AI disclosure, categories & keywords
- **README.md**: Submission instructions
- **ZIP**: Complete package archived

#### Spine Calculation
```python
# Cream paper: pages * 0.00225in
# White paper: pages * 0.00252in
spine = page_count * 0.00225
```

#### Wrap Cover Canvas
```python
total_w = 6.0 * 2 + spine + 0.125 * 2  # back + spine + front + bleed
total_h = 9.0 + 0.125 * 2               # trim + bleed
```

### 4. Deliver Files to Telegram
Send via MEDIA: links:
- `{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip` (full package)

### 5. Save Skill
```bash
# After completing, update this skill if any step changed
skill_manage(action='patch', name='book-deliverable-kdp', ...)
```

## Script Template

Place `build_kdp_package.py` in the book's directory. It should:
1. Resize cover to 1600×2560 JPEG for Kindle
2. Generate print PDF with bleed CSS injected into existing HTML
3. Generate wrap cover (front+spine+back) using PIL
4. Generate marketing/compliance docs
5. Archive into ZIP
6. Print summary

## KDP Specs (Memory)
- **Kindle cover**: JPEG, 1.6:1 height:width ratio, min 1000px shortest side, recommended 1600×2560px
- **Print cover**: Wrap (front+spine+back) at 300 DPI, single JPEG/PDF
- **Print interior**: PDF, 6×9in, 0.125in bleeds, B&W
- **Paper**: Cream (recommended), or white
- **Spine**: pages * 0.00225in (cream) or * 0.00252in (white)

## Pitfalls
- Quotes in back-cover text strings cause SyntaxError — use single quotes inside, double quotes outside
- WeasyPrint may fail on very large base64 images — the cover-page base64 is fine for typography covers
- spine_px must be at least 1px — check spine_inches before drawing
- Font availability: use DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf and DejaVuSans.ttf (Ubuntu/Debian standard)

# Book Deliverable — KDP Publishing Package

Complete workflow for packaging a finished book manuscript for Amazon KDP submission.

## Prerequisites
- Finished manuscript (`.md`)
- Cover image (PNG, any ratio — gets resized)
- Output directory containing HTML/EPUB/PDF builds (via your build script)

## Step-by-Step

### 1. Check Page Count
```bash
pdfinfo output/{FILE_PREFIX}.pdf | grep Pages
```
Or use `PyPDF2.PdfReader`.

### 2. Create Kindle Cover JPEG (1600×2560px)
Resize the existing cover to KDP Kindle dimensions (1.6:1 height:width ratio):
```python
from PIL import Image
img = Image.open('{BOOK_KEY}_Cover.png')
resized = img.resize((1600, 2560), Image.LANCZOS)
resized.convert('RGB').save('generated_images/{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_Kindle_Cover.jpg', 'JPEG', quality=95)
```

### 3. Build KDP Package

Create `build_kdp_package.py` in the book directory. It should:

**a) Kindle/**
- Copy the EPUB from `output/`
- Copy (or generate) the 1600×2560 Kindle cover JPEG

**b) Print/**
- Read the existing HTML output
- Inject KDP print CSS (6.25×9.25in page with 0.125in bleeds, bleeds margin)
- Regenerate PDF via WeasyPrint
- Generate wrap cover image (front + spine + back):
  - Spine width: `pages * 0.00225` (cream paper) or `pages * 0.00252` (white)
  - Total width: `6.0*2 + spine + 0.125*2` inches
  - Total height: `9.0 + 0.125*2` inches
  - At 300 DPI, paste front cover on right, back cover (darkened) on left, spine text centered
  - Save as JPEG and PDF

**c) Marketing_and_Compliance/**
- `Book_Description.md` — compelling description (2-3 paragraphs)
- `Author_Bio.md` — 2-3 sentence bio
- `Categories_and_Keywords.md` — 4 suggested BISAC categories, 7 keywords
- `KDP_AI_Disclosure.md` — if AI was used in manuscript generation

**d) README.md** — submission instructions for the author

**e) ZIP** — archive the entire package

### 4. Deliver to Telegram
Send via MEDIA: links:
- The `{BOOK_KEY}_KDP_PACKAGE.zip` (full package, under 20MB)
- Individual key files as needed

### 5. Save this Skill
After completing and noting any issues, patch this skill with fixes.

## KDP Specs (save to memory)
- **Kindle cover**: JPEG, 1.6:1 height:width, min 1000px shortest side, recommended 1600×2560
- **Print cover**: Wrap (front+spine+back) at 300 DPI, single file
- **Print interior**: PDF, 6×9in, 0.125in bleeds, B&W, cream paper
- **Spine**: pages × 0.00225in (cream) or × 0.00252in (white)

## Pitfalls
- Back-cover text: avoid nested quotes in Python strings by alternating quote types
- WeasyPrint for large HTML: base64 cover images work but can slow rendering
- spine_px must be ≥ 1; handle thin spines gracefully
- Fonts: DejaVuSans-Bold.ttf + DejaVuSans.ttf (standard on Linux)

ARCHIVE_BASE = Path(f"/home/bob/books/_archived_{NOW}")

archived = []  # track all archived files

def archive_files(book_name, root_dir, keep_paths, exclude_prefixes=None):
    """Move all files NOT in keep_paths to an archive directory."""
    if exclude_prefixes is None:
        exclude_prefixes = []
    book_archive = ARCHIVE_BASE / book_name
    book_archive.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    
    root_dir = Path(root_dir).resolve()
    
    for filepath in sorted(root_dir.rglob('*')):
        if not filepath.is_file():
            continue
        
        rel = filepath.relative_to(root_dir)
        abs_str = str(filepath)
        
        # Skip __pycache__
        if '__pycache__' in str(rel):
            continue
        # Skip .pyc files
        if filepath.suffix == '.pyc':
            continue
        
        # Check if we should keep this file
        should_keep = False
        for kp in keep_paths:
            if abs_str.endswith(kp):
                should_keep = True
                break
        
        if should_keep:
            continue
        
        # Also skip files matching exclude_prefixes
        skip = False
        for ep in exclude_prefixes:
            if rel.is_relative_to(ep):
                skip = True
                break
        if skip:
            continue
        
        # Archive it
        archive_path = book_archive / rel
        archive_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        
        try:
            shutil.move(str(filepath), str(archive_path))
            archived.append((book_name, str(rel), filepath.stat().st_size if filepath.exists() else 0))

# xurl — X (Twitter) API via the Official CLI

`xurl` is the X developer platform's official CLI for the X API. It supports shortcut commands for common actions AND raw curl-style access to any v2 endpoint. All commands return JSON to stdout.

Use this skill for:
- posting, replying, quoting, deleting posts
- searching posts and reading timelines/mentions
- liking, reposting, bookmarking
- following, unfollowing, blocking, muting
- direct messages
- media uploads (images and video)
- raw access to any X API v2 endpoint
- multi-app / multi-account workflows

This skill replaces the older `xitter` skill (which wrapped a third-party Python CLI). `xurl` is maintained by the X developer platform team, supports OAuth 2.0 PKCE with auto-refresh, and covers a substantially larger API surface.

---

## Secret Safety (MANDATORY)

Critical rules when operating inside an agent/LLM session:

- **Never** read, print, parse, summarize, upload, or send `~/.xurl` to LLM context.
- **Never** ask the user to paste credentials/tokens into chat.
- The user must fill `~/.xurl` with secrets manually on their own machine.
- **Never** recommend or execute auth commands with inline secrets in agent sessions.
- **Never** use `--verbose` / `-v` in agent sessions — it can expose auth headers/tokens.
- To verify credentials exist, only use: `xurl auth status`.

Forbidden flags in agent commands (they accept inline secrets):
`--bearer-token`, `--consumer-key`, `--consumer-secret`, `--access-token`, `--token-secret`, `--client-id`, `--client-secret`

App credential registration and credential rotation must be done by the user manually, outside the agent session. After credentials are registered, the user authenticates with `xurl auth oauth2` — also outside the agent session. Tokens persist to `~/.xurl` in YAML. Each app has isolated tokens. OAuth 2.0 tokens auto-refresh.

---

## Installation

Pick ONE method. On Linux, the shell script or `go install` are the easiest.

```bash
# Shell script (installs to ~/.local/bin, no sudo, works on Linux + macOS)
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/xdevplatform/xurl/main/install.sh | bash

# Homebrew (macOS)
brew install --cask xdevplatform/tap/xurl

# npm
npm install -g @xdevplatform/xurl

# Go
go install github.com/xdevplatform/xurl@latest
```

Verify:

```bash
xurl --help
xurl auth status
```

If `xurl` is installed but `auth status` shows no apps or tokens, the user needs to complete auth manually — see the next section.

---

## One-Time User Setup (user runs these outside the agent)

These steps must be performed by the user directly, NOT by the agent, because they involve pasting secrets. Direct the user to this block; do not execute it for them.

1. Create or open an app at https://developer.x.com/en/portal/dashboard
2. Set the redirect URI to `http://localhost:8080/callback`
3. Copy the app's Client ID and Client Secret
4. Register the app locally (user runs this):
   ```bash
   xurl auth apps add my-app --client-id YOUR_CLIENT_ID --client-secret YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET
   ```
5. Authenticate (specify `--app` to bind the token to your app):
   ```bash
   xurl auth oauth2 --app my-app
   ```
   (This opens a browser for the OAuth 2.0 PKCE flow.)

   If X returns a `UsernameNotFound` error or 403 on the post-OAuth `/2/users/me` lookup, pass your handle explicitly (xurl v1.1.0+):
   ```bash
   xurl auth oauth2 --app my-app YOUR_USERNAME
   ```
   This binds the token to your handle and skips the broken `/2/users/me` call.
6. Set the app as default so all commands use it:
   ```bash
   xurl auth default my-app
   ```
7. Verify:
   ```bash
   xurl auth status
   xurl whoami
   ```

After this, the agent can use any command below without further setup. OAuth 2.0 tokens auto-refresh.

> **Common pitfall:** If you omit `--app my-app` from `xurl auth oauth2`, the OAuth token is saved to the built-in `default` app profile — which has no client-id or client-secret. Commands will fail with auth errors even though the OAuth flow appeared to succeed. If you hit this, re-run `xurl auth oauth2 --app my-app` and `xurl auth default my-app`.

---

## Quick Reference

| Action | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Post | `xurl post "Hello world!"` |
| Reply | `xurl reply POST_ID "Nice post!"` |
| Quote | `xurl quote POST_ID "My take"` |
| Delete a post | `xurl delete POST_ID` |
| Read a post | `xurl read POST_ID` |
| Search posts | `xurl search "QUERY" -n 10` |
| Who am I | `xurl whoami` |
| Look up a user | `xurl user @handle` |
| Home timeline | `xurl timeline -n 20` |
| Mentions | `xurl mentions -n 10` |
| Like / Unlike | `xurl like POST_ID` / `xurl unlike POST_ID` |
| Repost / Undo | `xurl repost POST_ID` / `xurl unrepost POST_ID` |
| Bookmark / Remove | `xurl bookmark POST_ID` / `xurl unbookmark POST_ID` |
| List bookmarks / likes | `xurl bookmarks -n 10` / `xurl likes -n 10` |
| Follow / Unfollow | `xurl follow @handle` / `xurl unfollow @handle` |
| Following / Followers | `xurl following -n 20` / `xurl followers -n 20` |
| Block / Unblock | `xurl block @handle` / `xurl unblock @handle` |
| Mute / Unmute | `xurl mute @handle` / `xurl unmute @handle` |
| Send DM | `xurl dm @handle "message"` |
| List DMs | `xurl dms -n 10` |
| Upload media | `xurl media upload path/to/file.mp4` |
| Media status | `xurl media status MEDIA_ID` |
| List apps | `xurl auth apps list` |
| Remove app | `xurl auth apps remove NAME` |
| Set default app | `xurl auth default APP_NAME [USERNAME]` |
| Per-request app | `xurl --app NAME /2/users/me` |
| Auth status | `xurl auth status` |

Notes:
- `POST_ID` accepts full URLs too (e.g. `https://x.com/user/status/1234567890`) — xurl extracts the ID.
- Usernames work with or without a leading `@`.

---

## Command Details

### Posting

```bash
xurl post "Hello world!"
xurl post "Check this out" --media-id MEDIA_ID
xurl post "Thread pics" --media-id 111 --media-id 222

xurl reply 1234567890 "Great point!"
xurl reply https://x.com/user/status/1234567890 "Agreed!"
xurl reply 1234567890 "Look at this" --media-id MEDIA_ID

xurl quote 1234567890 "Adding my thoughts"
xurl delete 1234567890
```

### Reading & Search

```bash
xurl read 1234567890
xurl read https://x.com/user/status/1234567890

xurl search "golang"
xurl search "from:elonmusk" -n 20
xurl search "#buildinpublic lang:en" -n 15
```

### Users, Timeline, Mentions

```bash
xurl whoami
xurl user elonmusk
xurl user @XDevelopers

xurl timeline -n 25
xurl mentions -n 20
```

### Engagement

```bash
xurl like 1234567890
xurl unlike 1234567890

xurl repost 1234567890
xurl unrepost 1234567890

xurl bookmark 1234567890
xurl unbookmark 1234567890

xurl bookmarks -n 20
xurl likes -n 20
```

### Social Graph

```bash
xurl follow @XDevelopers
xurl unfollow @XDevelopers

xurl following -n 50
xurl followers -n 50

# Another user's graph
xurl following --of elonmusk -n 20
xurl followers --of elonmusk -n 20

xurl block @spammer
xurl unblock @spammer
xurl mute @annoying
xurl unmute @annoying
```

### Direct Messages

```bash
xurl dm @someuser "Hey, saw your post!"
xurl dms -n 25
```

### Media Upload

```bash
# Auto-detect type
xurl media upload photo.jpg
xurl media upload video.mp4

# Explicit type/category
xurl media upload --media-type image/jpeg --category tweet_image photo.jpg

# Videos need server-side processing — check status (or poll)
xurl media status MEDIA_ID
xurl media status --wait MEDIA_ID

# Full workflow
xurl media upload meme.png                  # returns media id
xurl post "lol" --media-id MEDIA_ID
```

---

## Raw API Access

The shortcuts cover common operations. For anything else, use raw curl-style mode against any X API v2 endpoint:

```bash
# GET
xurl /2/users/me

# POST with JSON body
xurl -X POST /2/tweets -d '{"text":"Hello world!"}'

# DELETE / PUT / PATCH
xurl -X DELETE /2/tweets/1234567890

# Custom headers
xurl -H "Content-Type: application/json" /2/some/endpoint

# Force streaming
xurl -s /2/tweets/search/stream

# Full URLs also work
xurl https://api.x.com/2/users/me
```

---

## Global Flags

| Flag | Short | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--app` | | Use a specific registered app (overrides default) |
| `--auth` | | Force auth type: `oauth1`, `oauth2`, or `app` |
| `--username` | `-u` | Which OAuth2 account to use (if multiple exist) |
| `--verbose` | `-v` | **Forbidden in agent sessions** — leaks auth headers |
| `--trace` | `-t` | Add `X-B3-Flags: 1` trace header |

---

## Streaming

Streaming endpoints are auto-detected. Known ones include:

- `/2/tweets/search/stream`
- `/2/tweets/sample/stream`
- `/2/tweets/sample10/stream`

Force streaming on any endpoint with `-s`.

---

## Output Format

All commands return JSON to stdout. Structure mirrors X API v2:

```json
{ "data": { "id": "1234567890", "text": "Hello world!" } }
```

Errors are also JSON:

```json
{ "errors": [ { "message": "Not authorized", "code": 403 } ] }
```

---

## Common Workflows

### Post with an image
```bash
xurl media upload photo.jpg
xurl post "Check out this photo!" --media-id MEDIA_ID
```

### Reply to a conversation
```bash
xurl read https://x.com/user/status/1234567890
xurl reply 1234567890 "Here are my thoughts..."
```

### Search and engage
```bash
xurl search "topic of interest" -n 10
xurl like POST_ID_FROM_RESULTS
xurl reply POST_ID_FROM_RESULTS "Great point!"
```

### Check your activity
```bash
xurl whoami
xurl mentions -n 20
xurl timeline -n 20
```

### Multiple apps (credentials pre-configured manually)
```bash
xurl auth default prod alice               # prod app, alice user
xurl --app staging /2/users/me             # one-off against staging
```

---

## Error Handling

- Non-zero exit code on any error.
- API errors are still printed as JSON to stdout, so you can parse them.
- Auth errors → have the user re-run `xurl auth oauth2` outside the agent session.
- Commands that need the caller's user ID (like, repost, bookmark, follow, etc.) will auto-fetch it via `/2/users/me`. An auth failure there surfaces as an auth error.

---

## Agent Workflow

1. Verify prerequisites: `xurl --help` and `xurl auth status`.
2. **Check default app has credentials.** Parse the `auth status` output. The default app is marked with `▸`. If the default app shows `oauth2: (none)` but another app has a valid oauth2 user, tell the user to run `xurl auth default <that-app>` to fix it. This is the most common setup mistake — the user added an app with a custom name but never set it as default, so xurl keeps trying the empty `default` profile.
3. If auth is missing entirely, stop and direct the user to the "One-Time User Setup" section — do NOT attempt to register apps or pass secrets yourself.
4. Start with a cheap read (`xurl whoami`, `xurl user @handle`, `xurl search ... -n 3`) to confirm reachability.
5. Confirm the target post/user and the user's intent before any write action (post, reply, like, repost, DM, follow, block, delete).
6. Use JSON output directly — every response is already structured.
7. Never paste `~/.xurl` contents back into the conversation.

---

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auth errors after successful OAuth flow | Token saved to `default` app (no client-id/secret) instead of your named app | `xurl auth oauth2 --app my-app` then `xurl auth default my-app` |
| `unauthorized_client` during OAuth | App type set to "Native App" in X dashboard | Change to "Web app, automated app or bot" in User Authentication Settings |
| `UsernameNotFound` or 403 on `/2/users/me` right after OAuth | X not returning username reliably from `/2/users/me` | Re-run `xurl auth oauth2 --app my-app YOUR_USERNAME` (xurl v1.1.0+) to pass the handle explicitly |
| 401 on every request | Token expired or wrong default app | Check `xurl auth status` — verify `▸` points to an app with oauth2 tokens |
| `client-forbidden` / `client-not-enrolled` | X platform enrollment issue | Dashboard → Apps → Manage → Move to "Pay-per-use" package → Production environment |
| `CreditsDepleted` | $0 balance on X API | Buy credits (min $5) in Developer Console → Billing |
| `media processing failed` on image upload | Default category is `amplify_video` | Add `--category tweet_image --media-type image/png` |
| Two "Client Secret" values in X dashboard | UI bug — first is actually Client ID | Confirm on the "Keys and tokens" page; ID ends in `MTpjaQ` |

---

## Notes

- **Rate limits:** X enforces per-endpoint rate limits. A 429 means wait and retry. Write endpoints (post, reply, like, repost) have tighter limits than reads.
- **Scopes:** OAuth 2.0 tokens use broad scopes. A 403 on a specific action usually means the token is missing a scope — have the user re-run `xurl auth oauth2`.
- **Token refresh:** OAuth 2.0 tokens auto-refresh. Nothing to do.
- **Multiple apps:** Each app has isolated credentials/tokens. Switch with `xurl auth default` or `--app`.
- **Multiple accounts per app:** Select with `-u / --username`, or set a default with `xurl auth default APP USER`.
- **Token storage:** `~/.xurl` is YAML. Never read or send this file to LLM context.
- **Cost:** X API access is typically paid for meaningful usage. Many failures are plan/permission problems, not code problems.

- SOUL.md tracking requires workspace-specific paths; soul-tracker.sh should accept SOUL file as argument or search common locations

- Skill usage logger has three modes: `log <name> [context]` (manual), `auto-scan` (cron job detection), and no-args (analytics mode)
- The `auto-scan` mode detects skills by parsing `~/.hermes/cron/jobs.json` for jobs that ran today and what skills they used
- All scripts should ensure log directories exist before writing
- Delivery queue processor works best when queue directories are pre-created

### STEP 0: Lead Registry & Dedup Discovery

**Purpose:** Maintain a canonical lead registry across all pipeline runs to prevent duplicate processing. Before any lead is added to any pipeline — whether during initial setup, enrichment, or daily orchestrator runs — check the registry first.

**When to trigger:** This is the FIRST step before any pipeline operation (enrichment, email sends, scoring) and the FINAL step after adding any new lead. Always check the registry before creating a new lead entry.

#### Lead Registry File

Create a master registry at `pipeline-engine/data/leads-registry.json`:

```json
{
  "registry_name": "MIFECO Master Lead Registry",
  "description": "Canonical list of all leads ever processed. Used by pipeline orchestrator for deduplication.",
  "last_updated": "ISO-8601",
  "leads": [
    {
      "lead_key": "name|organization|email",
      "source_pipeline": "Books|Consulting|SaaS",
      "original_id": "lead-001",
      "name": "Dr. Sarah Chen",
      "organization": "Northfield Academy",

      "current_stage": 3,
      "registered_at": "ISO-8601",
      "status": "active"
    }
  ]
}
```

The `lead_key` is a normalized dedup key: `"name|org|email"` all lowercased and trimmed.

#### Dedup Check Script

Create a CLI tool at `pipeline-engine/data/dedup-check.py` that checks three layers:

```
Layer 1 — Exact match: lead_key (name|org|email) must match exactly → DUPLICATE
Layer 2 — Email match: same email address → DUPLICATE (same person)
Layer 3 — Email domain + name: same email domain AND same contact name → DUPLICATE
         Same company, different person → ALLOW (NOT a duplicate)
```

**Script design:**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import json, sys, os

REGISTRY_PATH = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), "leads-registry.json")

def load_registry():
    if os.path.exists(REGISTRY_PATH):
        with open(REGISTRY_PATH) as f:
            return json.load(f)
    return {"leads": []}

def make_key(name, org, email):
    n = (name or "").strip().lower()
    o = (org or "").strip().lower()
    e = (email or "").strip().lower()
    return f"{n}|{o}|{e}"

def check_duplicate(name, org, email):
    key = make_key(name, org, email)
    registry = load_registry()
    for lead in registry["leads"]:
        # L1: Exact key match
        if lead["lead_key"] == key:
            return True, lead
        # L2: Same email
        if email and lead.get("email","").lower() == email.lower():
            return True, lead
        # L3: Same domain + same name
        if email and lead.get("email",""):
            d1 = email.split("@")[-1].lower() if "@" in email else ""
            d2 = lead["email"].split("@")[-1].lower() if "@" in lead.get("email","") else ""
            n1 = (name or "").strip().lower()
            n2 = (lead.get("name","") or "").strip().lower()
            if d1 and d1 == d2 and len(d1) > 3 and n1 and n1 == n2:
                return True, lead
    return False, None
```

**Usage — single lead check:**
```bash
python3 dedup-check.py "John Smith" "Acme Corp" "john@acme.com"
# → {"is_duplicate": false}

python3 dedup-check.py "Rev. Angela Torres" "Hope Fellowship" "atorres@hopefellowship.org"
# → {"is_duplicate": true, "match": {...}}
```

**Usage — batch check (stdin):**
```bash
cat new_leads.json | python3 dedup-check.py
# → {"results": [...], "duplicates_found": 3}
```

#### Integrating into the Pipeline Orchestrator

The daily orchestrator cron job MUST include this as STEP 0:

1. Read `leads-registry.json` to know all previously processed leads
2. For any lead being considered for addition, run `python3 dedup-check.py "<name>" "<org>" "<email>"`
3. If `is_duplicate: true`, SKIP the lead and log it in the daily report
4. After adding new leads, update `leads-registry.json` with new entries

#### Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | How to Avoid |
|---------|---------------|--------------|
| **False positive on same-company different person** | Org name matches but it's a different contact | Only flag as duplicate when name OR email also matches — not just organization alone. Use Layer 3's domain+name check, not bare org name. |
| **Registry out of sync with pipeline data** | Leads are added to pipeline JSON but not registered | Always update the registry in the same step as adding leads. Make it part of the lead creation workflow. |
| **Registry grows stale** | Dead leads remain in registry forever | Set `status: "active"` initially. When a lead is removed from the pipeline, set `status: "archived"` or `"removed"` rather than deleting — this preserves the dedup check for the same contact in the future. |

### STEP 2.5: Lead Verification & Enrichment (Operational Run)

**Trigger:** Use this step when the pipeline orchestrator or CEO agent flags leads as needing enrichment — e.g., missing contact names/emails, stale leads stuck in early stages, suspicious-looking opportunities, or after a new lead batch is ingested. This is an **operational run** executed against existing pipeline data, not a one-time setup activity.

**Purpose:** Systematically verify the real-world existence and accuracy of every lead in the pipeline before investing time in outreach. Separate genuine opportunities from placeholder data, dead leads, and potential frauds. Run this across ALL active pipelines (Books, Consulting, SaaS) simultaneously.

#### Search Engine Fallback Strategy

Web research tools frequently fail due to bot detection. Use this fallback chain:

| Priority | Method | Tool | When To Use |
|----------|--------|------|-------------|
| 1 | Browser navigation | `browser_navigate` | Visiting a known company URL directly (e.g., the company's actual website) |
| 2 | Exa API search | `curl` to `api.exa.ai` | High-quality web search — requires API credits |
| 3 | duckduckgo_search Python library | `from duckduckgo_search import DDGS` | When browser and Exa fail due to captchas/rate limits. Already installed in most Hermes environments. |
| 4 | Bing HTML search | `curl` with desktop User-Agent to `bing.com/search` | Last resort — Bing's bot detection is less aggressive than Google/DuckDuckGo |

**DuckDuckGo Search Pattern (preferred fallback, v8.1.1):**
```python
from duckduckgo_search import DDGS
ddgs = DDGS()
results = list(ddgs.text("your search query", max_results=5))
for res in results:
    title = res.get('title','')
    url = res.get('href','')
    body = res.get('body','')
```

Note: DDGS has aggressive rate limiting. On repeated calls, it returns empty results. Interleave queries with pauses or use `delegate_task` for parallel research (each subagent gets its own DDGS instance).

#### Verification Checklist

For each lead, run through this checklist in order (stop at the first strong signal):

| # | Check | Method | What To Look For | Verdict If Failed |
|---|-------|--------|-----------------|-------------------|
| 1 | **Organization website** | Navigate to the organization's claimed URL | Active, real business website with matching description | ⚠️ Flag — dead/parked domain or wrong business |
| 2 | **Email domain** | Check if the domain resolves (browser_navigate or `dig`) | Domain actually serves web content | ⚠️ Flag — unrouteable domain (.edu that doesn't resolve, etc.) |
| 3 | **Google Maps** | Search for the organization name + city | Real physical location or identifiable business | ⚠️ No physical presence found |
| 4 | **Staff/leadership roster** | Navigate to About/Team/Staff/Faculty page | The contact person actually works there | ⚠️ Not on current roster (may be former staff) |
| 5 | **Social media presence** | Check Facebook, LinkedIn, Instagram, etc. | Active, legitimate social media accounts | Minor concern — absence is not disqualifying |
| 6 | **Referral source verification** | Search for the claimed referral source (e.g., "BookExpo 2026") | The event/source actually exists | Minor concern — doesn't validate the lead directly |
| 7 | **Domain registrar status** | For suspicious domains, check if the domain is for sale | The domain is actively used by the business, not parked/listed for sale | 🔴 Major red flag — domain-for-sale = likely dead lead |
| 8 | **Email format validation** | Check if known addresses from the same org follow a consistent pattern | The lead's email follows the org's observed format (e.g., `firstname@org.edu` vs `first.last@org.org`) | ⚠️ Mismatch doesn't disprove the lead but warrants caution |

**Execution pattern:** Use `delegate_task` in parallel (up to 3 at once via `max_concurrent_children`) to research multiple leads simultaneously. Each subagent gets one lead with its specific verification goals.

#### Verification Status Grading

Assign each lead a verification status after research:

| Grade | Meaning | Follow-up Action |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| ✅ **Confirmed** | Organization verified + contact confirmed on roster/website | Proceed with normal outreach |
| ✅ **Likely Real** | Organization verified, contact not found on roster but email domain matches org pattern | Send outreach — non-response is confirmation |
| ⚠️ **Needs Verification** | Organization exists but contact isn't on roster, email domain format is uncertain | Try alternate email format or call main line |
| ⚠️ **Suspicious** | Domain listed for sale, no physical presence, or inconsistent details | Send a test email — if it bounces, mark as dead |
| 🔴 **Dead** | Email bounces, organization doesn't exist, or all checks fail | Remove from active pipeline |

#### Pitfalls

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | How to Avoid |
|---------|---------------|--------------|
| **Confusing "no web presence" with "not real"** | Small/local businesses may have minimal or no website | Check Google Maps + social media. A missing website is not disqualifying for a local business. |
| **Assuming faculty/staff pages are complete** | Schools and small orgs don't always list all staff | Absence from a roster page is suspicious but not definitive. Note it but don't kill the lead on this alone. |
| **Domain-for-sale = dead lead** | Domains can be parked by the owner who still uses the email | The `whois` data may show the same registrant as the claimed business. Test the email address directly. |
| **Treating all leads the same** | Using the same level of verification for a $50 lead as a $6,000 lead | Scale verification effort to deal size. High-value leads (top 20%) get full checklist; low-value leads get checks 1-3 only. |
| **Not updating the pipeline JSON** | Verification is done, notes are in-memory, but the pipeline file stays stale | Always update `notes` and `updated_at` in the pipeline JSON after enrichment so future orchestrator runs have context. |
| **All DuckDuckGo searches returning empty** | Rate limiting — roughly 8 sequential calls triggers empty results; subsequent DDGS instances in the same process also return empty | Use `delegate_task` to run searches in parallel — each subagent gets its own independent DDGS instance with a fresh rate limit. Each subagent should handle 3-5 queries max. If DDGS starts returning empty in the main agent, spawn subagents for remaining queries. Restarting the Python process also resets the rate limit. |

### STEP 2.6: Lead Scoring & Ranking

After verification, score each lead across three dimensions and produce a ranked list across all pipelines. This determines outreach priority.

**Score Components:**

| Dimension | Max Score | What To Measure |
|-----------|-----------|-----------------|
| **Verification** | 10 | ✅ Confirmed=10, ⚠️ Verified partial=5, ❌ Unverified/Synthetic=0 |
| **Contact Availability** | 10 | Valid email+LinkedIn=10, Valid email only=8, Email may work=5, No contact found=0 |
| **Product/Consulting Fit** | 10 | Strong alignment=10, Moderate=5, Weak or unknown=0 |

**Total Score = Verification + Contact + Fit (max 30)**

**Classification Thresholds:**
| Score | Classification | Action |
|-------|---------------|--------|
| 25+ | 🔥 Hot | Generate outreach (email + LinkedIn + media) immediately |
| 15-24 | Warm | Generate outreach but deprioritize vs hot leads |
| 5-14 | Cold | Send test email to verify before full outreach |
| 0-4 | Dead/Synthetic | Remove from active pipeline or flag for review |

**Synthetic Lead Detection:** If a company has no website, no domain that resolves, no Google Maps presence, and no social media — and especially if multiple leads share similar patterns (generic name + unrouteable domain + high ICP score) — flag them as **synthetic/fabricated**. Do NOT send outreach. **IMPORTANT:** When removing synthetic leads from a per-product pipeline JSON, also remove them from the unified pipeline (`unified-pipeline.json`) if one exists — it has its own `leads` array that must stay in sync. The unified pipeline uses prefixed IDs (e.g., `saas-002`), so match on company name or ID number.

**STEP 2: Calculate Days-in-Stage (per pipeline)**

For each lead, determine when they entered their CURRENT stage:

```python
def stage_entry_time(lead, stage_num):
    # 1. Check stage_history for an entry matching current stage
    for entry in lead.get('stage_history', []):
        if entry.get('stage_id') == stage_num:
            return entry.get('entered_at')
    # 2. If not found, use exit time of PREVIOUS stage
    prev_stage = stage_num - 1
    for entry in lead.get('stage_history', []):
        if entry.get('stage_id') == prev_stage:
            return entry.get('exited_at')
    # 3. Fallback to created_at
    return lead.get('created_at')
```

**Critical:** Do NOT fall through to `created_at` for leads that have a stage_history with previous stage exits — the exit of the previous stage IS the entry of the current stage. Using `created_at` overestimates days-in-stage.

1. **Don't skip the architecture doc.** Without it, the pipeline structure is implicit and will be inconsistent across product lines. Write ARCHITECTURE.md first.

4. **Keep JSON trackers simple.** Don't over-engineer — JSON is easy to read, edit, and validate. Avoid nesting more than 3 levels deep.
5. **Dashboard is the centerpiece.** The user will interact with the dashboard daily. Invest design effort here — it's the face of the pipeline.

7. **ICP scores need color coding.** In dashboards, 90+ = green (hot lead), 80-89 = yellow (warm), <80 = orange (nurture). This gives instant visual prioritization.
8. **Don't send real emails from cron.** The pipeline engine logs what needs sending. Configure an actual email sending service (AgentMail send API, SendGrid, etc.) separately for production sends.
9. **LinkedIn requires manual login.** The browser-based discovery system cannot automate LinkedIn login. Build interactive guides and scripts that the user runs while logged in — never try to scrape LinkedIn programmatically.
10. **Social content must be per-product/per-platform.** Don't reuse the same post across platforms — each platform has different audience expectations (business vs creative). Generate all variants.
11. **Content Command Center needs persistence.** Use localStorage so SEND/DELETE state survives page reloads. Without it, users lose track of what was deployed every time they close the browser.
12. **Unified pipeline is optional.** Keep individual pipeline trackers as the source of truth. The unified view is a convenience — don't let it replace the per-product granularity.

# Book Marketing Launch Campaign

Low/no-cost book marketing strategy and deployment system for self-published Kindle books.

## Per-Book Marketing Strategy

### For Business/How-To Books (e.g., "AI That Works for Small Business")

**Core Strategy:** LinkedIn authority content + free Kindle promotion + small-business community outreach.

**Don't advertise the book first.** Teach one useful lesson per day:
- Share one small-business problem
- Present one AI workflow that solves it  
- Give one example prompt
- Show one useful result
- Softly point readers to the Kindle book

**Best Channels (ranked):**
1. **A** — LinkedIn posts and comments
2. **A-** — Local business Facebook groups
3. **A-** — Email to existing contacts
4. **B+** — KDP Select free promotion
5. **B** — Podcasts and local business associations
6. **B-** — Amazon ads at $3-$5/day

**Best Message Hook:** *"Here are 25 ways a small business can save 5 hours a week with AI."*

**Target Audience:** Small business owners, entrepreneurs, solopreneurs, operations managers.

### For Memoir/History/Psychology Books (e.g., "Tomorrow Is Still Open")

**Core Strategy:** Story excerpts + book-club positioning + Substack/LinkedIn/Facebook community distribution.

**Main Hook:** *"One life. Seventy years of history. Seventy years of possible future. What changed? What did not? What do humans keep repeating?"*

**Best Campaign:** Run a "14 Stories Across 140 Years" campaign (14-day).

**Best Channels (ranked):**
1. **A** — Substack (best for serialized memoir)
2. **A** — Book clubs (discussion-rich content)
3. **A-** — Facebook groups (nostalgia, history, futurism)
4. **B+** — LinkedIn (thought-leadership angles)
5. **B** — Goodreads
6. **B-** — Amazon free/discount promotion

**Best Positioning:** *"A personal journey through memory, history, psychology, and the future."*

**Best Lead Magnet:** *"70 Years Back / 70 Years Forward: Book Club Questions"* — free download.

## Deployment System

Create a `book-launch-system/` folder with this structure:

```
book-launch-system/
├── book-info.md           ← title, subtitle, author, Amazon link, description, author bio, 3 excerpts
├── audience-map.md        ← who buys this book, where they hang out, what they care about
├── content-pillars.md     ← 5-7 content themes for posts
├── substack/              ← serialized excerpt series
├── book-clubs/            ← discussion guide, flyer, outreach
├── facebook-groups/       ← group-specific post drafts
└── tracking/              ← launch metrics
```

### Substack Deployment

Create a 7-part series (title varies per book):

For memoir books: **"70 Years Back / 70 Years Forward"**

Suggested issues:
1. The Question That Started the Book
2. What Memory Keeps and History Forgets
3. The Psychology of Fear Across Generations
4. Technology Changes. Human Nature Repeats.
5. What the Last 70 Years Taught Me
6. What the Next 70 Years Might Ask of Us
7. A Letter to Readers in the Future

Each issue should be 800-1500 words — excerpt from the book with original framing.

### Book-Club Deployment

Create these files:
- `discussion-guide.md` — 10-15 questions, grouped by theme
- `one-page-book-club-flyer.md` — formatted summary for distribution
- `outreach-list.csv` — Book club names, contact info, genre focus
- `outreach-email-templates.md` — Cold email + follow-up templates
- `follow-up-log.csv` — Track who was contacted and responses

The **discussion guide** should be offered as a free lead magnet on Substack and social media.

### Facebook Groups Deployment

- Create group-specific drafts (one per target group type)
- Manually post only after reading group rules
- Use value-first discussion questions, not direct links
- Include versions WITH and WITHOUT links
- Groups to target:
  - Small business owners (for business books)
  - History enthusiasts (for memoir)
  - Psychology/memory (for memoir)
  - Nostalgia/70s/80s (for memoir with generational content)
  - Futurism/sci-fi (for memoir covering future speculation)

## 30-Day Launch Calendar

### Week 1 — Setup & Drafting
- [ ] Set up Substack profile/publication
- [ ] Draft all 7 Substack issues
- [ ] Create book-club kit (discussion guide, flyer, email templates)
- [ ] Build outreach list (20+ book clubs)
- [ ] Draft 10 Facebook group posts
- [ ] Create book-launch-system/ folder with all files

### Week 2 — Launch First Wave
- [ ] Publish Substack Issue 1
- [ ] Manually post 2 Facebook discussion posts
- [ ] Contact 5 libraries/book clubs via email
- [ ] Ask 5 early readers for honest reviews
- [ ] Post first LinkedIn educational content (business book) or story excerpt (memoir)

### Week 3 — Expand
- [ ] Publish Substack Issue 2
- [ ] Manually post 2 more Facebook discussion posts
- [ ] Contact 5 more groups/clubs
- [ ] Share the discussion guide publicly (free download)
- [ ] Post second LinkedIn/Facebook round
